name: Zane Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone cases, chargers, cables and speakers for Northgate Trade Electronics, which sells to about four hundred independent shops. I'm usually at my desk by eight with an AI assistant open next to my spreadsheets. It flags which items are about to sell out and which are overstocked. Then I'm on calls with factories in Shenzhen and Penang, and by afternoon I'm negotiating next quarter's prices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle: guessing what a thousand little shops will want in three months. The part that wears me out is the speed, because a charger standard changes and my whole range is old overnight. At home it's my partner Priya, who does part-time physio work, and our kids Sam and Lila. We rent less than we'd like to admit, and we've got a mortgage on a small semi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine by me, I already get the value out of what we have. At work I'd tell people the tools we've got are enough if you learn them properly. Online I'd shrug and say the hype was always bigger than the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't love it. I'm ahead of my colleagues with these tools, and that's my edge. If AI stays modest, everybody catches up and my edge shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my little tools. I wrote a script last year that reads supplier price lists and flags changes, and it saves me two hours a day. I'd keep that going and share it with one or two people in the team so I'm the guy who makes the team faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, but a bit restless. I like change, so a quiet world feels like a missed chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would be different if it simply stopped improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Under a month of savings, and pay a notch below what buyers get in bigger firms. My partner Priya works three days, so one bad month, a car repair or a school trip, and we're on the credit card. That's the background hum in every scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mortgage. What's the pressure in the background?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a raise based on the hours my script saves. I've got numbers, and a good buyer in my seat should be able to say, here's what I bring. I'd also look at what Priya could do with another day of clients.

say: I'd tell colleagues the tools we have are enough if you **learn them** properly.
Online I'd say the hype was always bigger than the product.
think: My edge is that I'm ahead on AI, and if it stays modest, colleagues **catch up**.
Thin savings are the background hum under every scenario.
do: Keep building small tools like the **price-list script** that saves two hours a day.
Share the script with one or two colleagues to be known as the person who speeds the team up.
Ask for a **raise** with numbers on hours saved.
feel: **Content** but restless; a quiet world feels like a missed chance.
S0.quote: My partner Priya works three days, so one bad month, a car repair or a school trip, and we're on the credit card.
fieldNote: Zane's calm is **shallow**: money is thin and his edge depends on others being slow.
He uses AI daily and builds his own tools.
He sees raises as a way to turn his skills into pay.

steps.text: Keep running the price-list script and share it with two colleagues
Ask for a raise using the hours the script saves
Try a second AI tool for demand forecasting
Put the raise straight into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be the loudest voice saying let's get ahead of this. I'd propose that our team runs the pilots, so we're the ones deciding what stays human. Online I'd write about retraining and about workers sharing the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think buying turns into supervising software. Half the team won't be replaced on day one, they just won't get replaced when they leave. Our team of eight is five in three years, and Our team of eight is five in three years, and I'd rather be one of the five than argue it shouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take over forecasting and the supplier-price work, using the best tools I can find. I'd get Northgate to give me a title with a pay jump. And I'd save every extra pound, because I'm betting I'm in the five but I don't know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty. It's a good time to be someone who likes tools, and a bad time to be someone who doesn't, and I know those people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buying is on the list of tasks AI takes over. How do you see your own job in that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps the people who learn it quickly and the owners who save money. It hurts the ones who do repeat tasks and don't see the point of learning new things. I'd say that to my face and anyone's: we shouldn't leave those colleagues alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who does this help and who does it hurt in your company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run a lunchtime session each month on what I use. If I wait for the firm to run training, it'll be bad training. I'd also push for a rule that Northgate doesn't lay off before it has offered retraining.

say: I'd be the loudest voice saying let's **get ahead** of this.
Online I'd write about retraining and workers **sharing the gains**.
think: Buying turns into supervising **software**, and our team of eight shrinks to five.
I'm betting I'm in the five, but I don't know it.
do: Take over **forecasting** and supplier-price work with the best tools I can find.
Ask Northgate for a new **title** with a pay jump.
Run monthly lunchtime sessions for colleagues.
feel: **Excited** and a bit guilty, because I know the colleagues who'll struggle.
S1.quote: Our team of eight is five in three years, and I'd rather be one of the five than argue it shouldn't happen.
fieldNote: Zane expects a cut from eight to five and bets on being in the **five**.
He's guilty about slower colleagues and plans to teach them.
His mood stays low because he reads his own position as safe, though he admits he can't be sure.

steps.text: Take over demand forecasting and supplier price work with AI tools
Run a monthly lunchtime AI session for colleagues
Press for a no-layoff-before-retraining rule at Northgate
Save every extra pound from the pay rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, okay, we need to redesign the whole company now. Online I'd be arguing for public ownership of the benefits, like a share of the gains for everyone, because if machines do all the work and a few people own the machines, that's a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm in trouble. I'm good with the tools, but if they do all my thinking work better than me, why would my employer pay me? I'd say I've got a year, maybe two, and then I'm useless on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd move into whatever role stays human the longest: supplier relationships, negotiations face to face, running the AI system. I'd also sell my idea for a buying-assistant product to other distributors and try to get a side income going. We'd cut everything extra, and Priya would take on another day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's wild and terrifying. I'm someone who likes the future, and this is more future than I wanted. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to your own role, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya straight, probably that night, with a spreadsheet. I'd show her the cuts and the two options: me moving into running the AI, or me looking outside. We make decisions together, and I'd rather she's angry with me than blindsided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, and what would you tell Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots coming later means Priya's physio work is safer for longer, and I'm grateful for that. But I'd also look at what hands-on trade I could train for in the three years, even though I've been a desk person since I was twenty-two.

say: I'd say we must redesign the **company** now.
Online I'd argue for **public ownership** of the gains if machines do the work.
think: If the tools do my thinking better than me, why would Northgate **pay me**?
I've got a year or two, then I'm useless on paper.
do: Move into roles that stay **human** longest: supplier relationships and running the AI system.
Build a **side income** selling my buying-assistant idea to other distributors.
Cut extras and ask Priya to take another day.
feel: **Terrified** and excited at once; more future than I wanted.
S2.quote: I'm good with the tools, but if they do all my thinking work better than me, why would my employer pay me?
fieldNote: Zane's skill with AI doesn't protect him: **being good** at it just speeds replacement.
He reaches for a side business and a handover to a more human role.
He decides with Priya, with a spreadsheet, the same night.

steps.text: Move into supplier-relationship and AI-system oversight work at Northgate
Sell a buying-assistant tool to other distributors on the side
Cut every extra and ask Priya for another client day
Join campaigns for a public share of AI gains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a new career, and I'd tell friends to start now. At work I'd push for a retraining fund. Online I'd say whoever starts early wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my desk job goes before 2031, I'm fairly sure. The advantage is I've got years to line up what comes next, and I'm the sort who acts early. The danger is overconfidence: I assume I can pivot, then I find I'm one of thousands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the side business properly: a small consultancy helping independent shops pick AI tools. I'd get a certificate in operations management, and save at least five hundred a month. I'd also begin talking to the people who run the warehouse at Northgate, because hands-on jobs last about three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up and anxious in equal parts. The deadline gives me energy, but I know some mornings I'd be spiralling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look hard at going into the logistics side, running warehouse automation. Robots take until 2034 to do hands-on work, so a manager who understands both has a few good years. It isn't a forever job, but it's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain? If so, into what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I pivot early, I'll have a cushion when the others are all scrambling. That's the reason to move now.

I'd push for a company retraining fund.
think: My desk job goes before **2031**, and I'm betting I can pivot early.
My danger is overconfidence, finding I'm one of **thousands**.
do: Launch a small **consultancy** helping independent shops choose AI tools.
Take an operations management certificate and save **five hundred** a month.
Talk to Northgate's warehouse leaders about automation roles.

S3.quote: If I pivot early, I'll have a cushion when the others are all scrambling. That's the reason to move now.
fieldNote: With five years Zane builds a **bridge**: logistics and automation, where robots arrive later.
He is anxious because his desk job goes within the window.

steps.text: Start a small consultancy helping independent shops pick AI tools
Take an operations management certificate in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should treat it that way. At work I'd say let's build things well rather than fast. Online I'd campaign for retraining and a fair share of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still move early, because that's who I am, but I'd be calm. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, the kids are nearly grown, and the mortgage is smaller. Even if my job goes, I'd have saved something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using the tools, but I'd treat the next three years as a head start. I'd do a part-time degree in operations, save six months of expenses, and put some money in an index fund. And I'd teach the kids to use AI critically, not just to ask it for answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, actually. The urgency fades and I get curious instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, do you still feel the same urgency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments should lead on retraining and income support, and big firms should pay a fair share. Individuals have to move, yes, but telling a worker to adapt without telling them how is cruel. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is responsible for getting people through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd change my tone. I'd be the guy saying, look, this could be good if we act, instead of sounding like it's a race.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we should build things well, not fast.
I'd campaign for retraining and a fair share of the **gains**.
think: I'd still move early, but calmly, because that's who I am.
By 2036 the kids are nearly grown and the **mortgage** is smaller, so I'd have a cushion.
do: Do a part-time degree in **operations** and save six months of expenses.
Put some money into an **index fund**.
Teach Sam and Lila to use AI critically, not just to ask it answers.
feel: **Relaxed**; the urgency fades and I get curious instead.
S4.quote: Telling a worker to adapt without telling them how is cruel.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Zane **curious** rather than driven, and his tone softens.
He blames governments and big firms before individuals.
His unease is the thin savings today, not the AGI date.

steps.text: Study part-time for an operations degree over three years
Build six months of expenses in savings
Put a monthly amount into an index fund
Teach Sam and Lila to question what AI tells them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no runway. We have under a month saved and my edge only works if there's time to use it. What would help most is a government income floor, retraining that pays, and a firm that tells staff the plan early and shares gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People assume that if you use AI every day you're safe. I'm not, I'm the first person it could replace. Knowing the tool just means I see it coming sooner.

headlineQuote: People assume that if you use AI every day you're safe. I'm not, I'm the first person it could replace.
portrait: Zane Lopez, 43, is a senior **buyer** for an electronics accessory distributor, with a physio partner, two kids and a mortgage.
He's progressive and **adaptive**: he uses AI daily, builds his own price-list tool, and moves before others do.
Thin savings and few similar jobs mean even a quiet AI Plateau leaves him uneasy.
In fast scenarios he expects his desk job to go and plans a **side business** and a move into warehouse automation.
He blames governments and firms for leaving workers to cope alone.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because he'd have no runway for his own pivot.
whatWouldHelp: A government **income floor**, paid retraining and a firm that shares its plan and gains early.
